trivia: Elias Garcia Martinez painted a competent, forgettable Christ on a church wall in Borja in about two sittings, and it stayed unremarkable for eighty-two years. Then an elderly parishioner named Cecilia Gimenez, worried about the flaking, began restoring it herself and produced what the internet immediately christened Ecce Mono, Behold the Monkey. The original painter's own granddaughter had donated money toward that restoration, which is the detail that makes the whole thing unbearable. What happened next is the good part: a town of a few thousand went from no visitors to tens of thousands, started charging admission, built an interpretation centre and negotiated Gimenez a share of the proceeds. There is now an opera about it. She has said she never meant to finish it that day and simply ran out of time. Note that the card shows the 2012 state of a 1930 painting, the way the Night Watch is still dated 1642 despite being cut down in 1715.

title: American Gothic
trivia: The models were Wood's dentist and his own sister Nan, who was so annoyed at being taken for the farmer's wife that she spent the rest of her life correcting people, insisting she was the daughter. Iowans wrote furious letters saying it made them look grim and pinched; one farm wife threatened to bite Wood's ear off. It won a $300 prize and has been parodied more than almost any painting alive.

title: Composition II in Red, Blue, and Yellow
trivia: Mondrian refused to use green and reportedly turned his chair away from a window in a friend's studio because there were too many trees outside it. He arrived at pure grids after years of painting increasingly abstract trees, so the whole system grew out of the thing he later banned. He also loved dancing, was an enthusiastic Charleston devotee, and split from the De Stijl group when a colleague introduced diagonal lines.

title: The Persistence of Memory
location: Museum of Modern Art, New York
trivia: Dalí claimed the soft watches came from staring at a runny Camembert after dinner and finishing the painting in a couple of hours while Gala was at the cinema. She came back and said nobody who saw it would forget it. The fleshy shape in the centre is a distorted self-portrait profile that appears in several of his paintings. It is smaller than most people expect, about 24 by 33 centimetres.

title: Henry Ford Hospital
trivia: Painted in Detroit in the weeks after a miscarriage, on a sheet of metal because that was what was available and because Mexican devotional ex-votos were painted on metal too. She is on a hospital bed floating in an empty industrial landscape with the Ford plant on the horizon, connected by red ribbons to six objects including a foetus and a machine part. Kahlo was 25, and this is where her mature work begins.

title: Migrant Mother
trivia: Lange shot six frames in about ten minutes at a pea-pickers' camp in California, working for a government relief agency, and the photograph prompted federal food aid to be sent within days. The woman, Florence Owens Thompson, was not identified publicly for forty years and was unhappy about it, saying she had never received anything from a picture that made everyone else money. A thumb in an early frame was retouched out.

title: Guernica
trivia: Picasso refused to let it enter Spain while Franco lived, and it hung at MoMA for decades on that condition, finally arriving in Madrid in 1981. The town was bombed by German and Italian aircraft supporting Franco; Picasso, in Paris, read the newspaper reports and started within days. A tapestry copy hangs at the UN, and in 2003 it was covered with a curtain during a press conference about Iraq, which nobody has ever adequately explained.

title: Metamorphosis of Narcissus
trivia: Dalí took the canvas to London to show Freud in person, along with an accompanying poem. Freud, who had spent years dismissing Surrealists as cranks, wrote afterwards that he had been wrong and that this young Spaniard had changed his mind. Dalí sketched Freud during the meeting. The painting works as a single visual pun: the crouching figure on the left is also the stone hand holding an egg on the right.

title: The Two Fridas
location: Museo de Arte Moderno, Mexico City
trivia: Painted in the year she divorced Diego Rivera, and by a wide margin her largest canvas. Two versions of herself sit holding hands, one in European dress with a severed artery bleeding onto her lap, one in Tehuana costume holding a small portrait of Diego as a child. Kahlo had a lifelong interest in medical illustration after a streetcar accident at 18 that left her in pain permanently. She and Rivera remarried a year later.

title: Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird
trivia: The dead hummingbird is a Mexican folk charm for luck in love, worn here as a wound, with the thorns drawing blood at her throat. The black cat behind one shoulder and the monkey Rivera gave her behind the other pull in opposite directions. It was painted for her lover, the photographer Nickolas Muray, and he took it back to New York. Kahlo sold few paintings in her lifetime and had one solo show in Mexico, attending it in a bed.

title: Nighthawks
trivia: Painted in the weeks after Pearl Harbor, and Hopper said only that he was probably painting the loneliness of a large city, then spent decades refusing to elaborate on anything. There is no door into the diner. His wife Jo modelled for the woman and kept the ledger recording the painting's details in her own handwriting. The Art Institute bought it for $3,000 within months. The diner was invented from a composite of Greenwich Avenue corners.

title: Freedom from Want
trivia: One of four paintings illustrating Roosevelt's Four Freedoms speech, published in the Saturday Evening Post with accompanying essays, then sent on a national tour that raised roughly $130 million in war bonds. Rockwell used his own family and neighbours and painted the turkey from the actual Thanksgiving bird his cook prepared. Europeans complained at the time that a table groaning with food was a strange advertisement for freedom from want.

title: Broadway Boogie Woogie
location: Museum of Modern Art, New York
trivia: Mondrian fled to New York in 1940 after the London studio next to his was bombed, discovered boogie-woogie records and immediately loved them, and broke his own famous black lines into pulsing coloured segments. He was 71 and it is his last completed painting. He worked on it for months, moving small pieces of coloured tape around the canvas before committing, and visitors described the studio itself as one of his compositions.

title: Three Studies for Figures at the Base of a Crucifixion
trivia: Shown in London in April 1945, in the same weeks the first photographs from Belsen and Buchenwald were appearing in British newspapers, and viewers reportedly left the room. Bacon later said the exhibition made his name and that he had destroyed nearly all his earlier work. The figures are based on the Furies. He painted on the unprimed reverse of the canvas, which meant the paint could never be corrected once applied.

title: Man Pointing
trivia: Giacometti made the original plaster overnight, in a single session, because it had been promised for an exhibition the following morning, and he later said he worked on it from midnight until nine. He habitually reduced his figures until almost nothing was left, and described this as trying to sculpt what he actually saw rather than what he knew was there. His brother Diego sat for most of the figures and also made the frames.

title: Christina's World
location: Museum of Modern Art, New York
trivia: MoMA bought it for $1,800 and critics spent the next thirty years filing Wyeth under illustration rather than art, a dismissal that only really softened after his death. Christina Olson was Wyeth's neighbour in Maine, had an undiagnosed degenerative muscular condition and could not walk, and was 55 when he painted her; the body in the picture is his wife's. She crawled around the property by choice, refusing a wheelchair.

title: Number 5, 1948
trivia: Life magazine ran a feature in 1949 asking whether Pollock was the greatest living painter in the United States, and the question, phrased sceptically, made him famous almost overnight and he never really recovered from it. He worked on the floor with the canvas unstretched, using hardened brushes, sticks and syringes. He died in 1956 driving drunk near his home, killing one passenger. He had been sober for two years before relapsing.

title: Drawing Hands
trivia: Escher trained as an architectural draughtsman, failed most of his school subjects and considered himself closer to a mathematician than an artist, which is roughly how the art world saw him too. He corresponded with the geometer Coxeter and the crystallographer Penrose. Mick Jagger once wrote asking to use an image on an album cover and addressed him informally; Escher declined and objected to being called Maurits by a stranger.

title: Autumn Rhythm (Number 30)
location: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
trivia: Hans Namuth's photographs and films of Pollock working, made that year, did more for his reputation than any exhibition, and also made him miserable, since he felt he was performing rather than painting. The shoot ended in a furious argument after which Pollock started drinking again. The painting is nearly five metres wide, made with commercial house enamel poured and flung, and there is almost no brush contact anywhere on it.

title: White Center (Yellow, Pink and Lavender on Rose)
trivia: David Rockefeller bought this in 1960 for about $10,000 on the advice of MoMA's curators and hung it in his office for nearly fifty years; it sold in 2007 for $72.8 million. Rothko specified that his paintings be hung low, in dim light, and viewed from around 45 centimetres away, and wrote angry letters when galleries ignored him. He rejected the label abstract painter entirely, insisting he was interested only in tragedy, ecstasy and doom, and that anyone who wept in front of the canvases was having the same experience he had while making them. The best illustration of how seriously he meant that came in 1958, when he took an enormous commission for a luxury restaurant in the Seagram Building, told a journalist he hoped to ruin the appetite of every rich diner in the room, ate there once, was disgusted and returned the money.

title: Christ of Saint John of the Cross
trivia: A visitor attacked it with a stone and tore it with his hands in 1961; it was repaired over several months. Glasgow had bought it for £8,200 amid furious local objections that the money should have gone to living Scottish artists, and it has since become the city's most popular possession. Dalí based the viewpoint on a drawing by the sixteenth-century mystic John of the Cross, and hired a Hollywood stuntman to hang from a gantry as the model.

title: Woman I
location: Museum of Modern Art, New York
trivia: De Kooning scraped it down and restarted for roughly two years, produced dozens of destroyed versions, and had actually thrown the canvas out before the critic Meyer Schapiro asked to see it and talked him into continuing. He said the grin came partly from a magazine advertisement for cigarettes he had pinned to the canvas. Feminist critics have attacked the series for decades; de Kooning claimed the figures made him laugh.

title: Study after Velázquez's Portrait of Pope Innocent X
trivia: Bacon painted around forty-five variations on the Velázquez and never once went to see the original, even when he was in Rome, which he explained by saying he did not want to spoil the reproductions he worked from. The scream is lifted partly from a still of the nurse in Eisenstein's Battleship Potemkin and partly from a medical textbook on diseases of the mouth that he kept for its colour plates.

title: Relativity
trivia: Three gravitational fields coexist in one building, each with its own floor and its own inhabitants, and each staircase is being used by people from two different worlds who cannot see each other. Escher worked it out geometrically before drawing. The image has been rebuilt in Lego, recreated in Labyrinth and Inception, and used in more computer-science lectures than probably any other picture.

title: No. 61 (Rust and Blue)
trivia: Rothko specified that his paintings be hung low, in dim light, and viewed from about 45 centimetres away, and wrote angry letters when galleries ignored him. He rejected being called an abstract painter and insisted he was interested only in tragedy, ecstasy and doom, adding that people who wept in front of the paintings were having the same religious experience he had while painting them. He also refused to explain what any of them meant.

title: Flag
date_note: 1954-55; inscribed 1954 on the reverse. Johns painted the motif for decades - this is the MoMA canvas
location: Museum of Modern Art, New York
trivia: Johns was 24 and painted it in hot pigmented wax over strips of torn newspaper after dreaming about the flag, which means the surface is full of half-legible 1950s headlines. It is deliberately unresolvable: a painting of a flag is also a flag. He had recently destroyed almost all his earlier work. MoMA hesitated to buy it in the McCarthy era in case it was read as unpatriotic, and had a collector purchase it as a proxy.

title: Just what is it that makes today's homes so different, so appealing?
trivia: A small collage made as a poster and catalogue image for a London exhibition, containing the word POP on a lollipop years before Pop art existed as a term. Hamilton assembled it from American magazines in an afternoon, working from a list he had written of what should be in it: man, woman, food, newspapers, cinema, comics, cars, appliances. Britain was still under food rationing memories, and the imagery was aspirational science fiction.

title: Monogram
trivia: Rauschenberg bought the stuffed angora goat from a second-hand office furniture shop on Seventh Avenue for $15, negotiated down from $35, and then spent four years failing to make it work in three separate versions before putting the tyre around its middle. He also repaired the goat's face with paint. It is now the single most famous object in Sweden's modern art museum, which bought it in 1965 for around $30,000.

title: Anthropometry of the Blue Period
trivia: Performed before a black-tie audience with an orchestra playing one single sustained note for twenty minutes followed by twenty minutes of silence, while models coated in Klein's patented blue pressed themselves onto paper at his direction. He wore a dinner jacket and never touched the paint. He patented the pigment formula as International Klein Blue. He died of a heart attack at 34, having had three in one month.

title: Movement in Squares
trivia: Riley was working as a commercial illustrator in an advertising agency when she painted this, and the compression down the centre reads as a fold in a flat surface that is not there. Op art became a fashion craze almost immediately; an American dress manufacturer copied her work onto fabric and she flew to New York to sue, discovered US copyright would not protect her, and campaigned about it for years afterwards.

title: Campbell's Soup Cans
location: Museum of Modern Art, New York
trivia: Thirty-two canvases, one for every variety the company sold that year, first shown propped on a shelf running around the gallery like a supermarket aisle. A nearby dealer stacked real cans in his window with a sign offering the genuine article cheaper. Five sold, and Warhol bought them back to keep the set together. Campbell's, after a nervous internal discussion, decided not to sue and later sent him a case of tomato soup.

title: Marilyn Diptych
date_note: card image must show BOTH panels - left colour, right black and white
trivia: Monroe died on 4 August 1962, in the same month Warhol first started experimenting with screenprinting, and over the following four months he made more than twenty paintings of her, every one built from a single cropped publicity still that Gene Kornman had shot for the 1953 film Niagara. The famous part is the left half in saturated colour against the right half fading into smeared black and white, universally read as celebrity against mortality. What is less often mentioned is that these were two separate paintings. The collectors Burton and Emily Tremaine came to the studio, were shown the black Marilyns first and the coloured one several pictures later, and Emily suggested hanging them as a diptych; Warhol's recorded response was gee whiz yes. So the most quoted interpretation in twentieth-century American painting rests on an arrangement the buyer thought of.

title: Whaam!
trivia: Lifted almost directly from a 1962 DC war comic drawn by Irv Novick, who was never credited or paid, and who had reportedly been Lichtenstein's superior officer during the war. The two-canvas format splits cause from effect. Lichtenstein enlarged the Ben-Day dots by hand using a stencil, so the mechanical look is entirely handmade. The Tate bought it in 1966, provoking complaints in Parliament about wasting public money.

title: Drowning Girl
location: Museum of Modern Art, New York
trivia: Lichtenstein cropped a full comic panel down to a single head, deleted the boyfriend swimming toward her in the original, and rewrote the caption so she would rather drown than call him. The source was a DC romance comic. The wave is borrowed, deliberately, from Hokusai. His father-in-law reportedly asked whether he was ever going to paint anything of his own.

title: Pope Leo X (after Raphael)
trivia: Botero took Raphael's 1518 portrait of Leo X, a painting the pope commissioned specifically so posterity would remember him with dignity, and turned him into something between an infant and a bureaucrat: round face, tiny features, stubby hands. Botero always insisted the inflation was about volume and sensuality rather than fat, and he had spent two years at a school for matadors before deciding on painting. Then in 2014 somebody put it on Reddit with the caption y tho, and it became the internet's standard reaction image for anything absurd or pointless. Botero died in 2023 with the obituaries split between his monumental public sculptures and the fact that he was, technically, the creator of a meme.

title: The Problem We All Live With
trivia: Rockwell had just left the Saturday Evening Post after 47 years, partly because its policy forbade depicting Black people except in service roles. Freed from it at 70, he painted six-year-old Ruby Bridges walking to school past a wall smeared with a thrown tomato and a racial slur, escorted by federal marshals whose heads are cropped out of frame. Obama had it hung outside the Oval Office in 2011 and met Bridges in front of it.

title: The Son of Man
trivia: Magritte described it as a self-portrait, and said the interesting thing is that we always want to see what is hidden by what we see, that there is an interest in what is concealed and what the visible does not show us. He painted the same idea repeatedly with apples, birds and flowers over faces. It has since been used in The Thomas Crown Affair, on album covers, and in roughly every advertisement about hidden potential.

title: Infinity Mirror Room - Phalli's Field
trivia: Kusama filled a mirrored room with hundreds of hand-sewn stuffed protrusions and photographed herself lying among them in a red leotard. She has described her work as coming directly from hallucinations she has experienced since childhood, in which patterns spread across surfaces and threaten to obliterate her. She has voluntarily lived in a Tokyo psychiatric hospital since 1977 and walks to her studio across the street to work every day.

title: A Bigger Splash
trivia: The splash took Hockney around two weeks to paint with small brushes, far longer than the flat blocks of building, pool and sky that surround it, which he did quickly with rollers. He liked the idea of spending that much time on something that lasts two seconds. He had moved to Los Angeles in 1964 and was struck that nobody in England had swimming pools while in California they were merely normal.

title: Spiral Jetty
trivia: Smithson chose the site partly because the water there is stained red by salt-tolerant bacteria, and built the 460-metre coil from 6,000 tonnes of basalt using hired dump trucks. It vanished under rising lake water within two years and stayed submerged for three decades before reappearing in the early 2000s, encrusted in white salt. Smithson died in a plane crash in 1973 at 35 while surveying another site from the air.

title: Diving (Olympische Spiele München 1972)
date_note: printed 1970-71 ahead of the Games; copyright line reads 1970 or 1971 depending on the run
trivia: Planning for the Munich art poster series began in 1967, and the organisers deliberately went to the best artists of the day rather than to designers: the full project ran to five series of seven posters each, with Hockney's in the third. He gave them a diver mid-entry into a pool, which is simply his California swimming-pool obsession of the late 1960s handed a public commission. Roughly half the run was printed in Germany, with his plate signature inside the image area, and half in the US with the signature below it, so the position of the signature tells you which side of the Atlantic a given copy came from. The Games themselves were meant to present a relaxed, democratic West Germany, an intention destroyed by the massacre of Israeli athletes three weeks after they opened. This copy hangs in the owner's apartment.

title: Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)
trivia: Hockney worked on a first version for six months and destroyed it, then finished the second in two frantic weeks before an exhibition deadline, working eighteen-hour days. The standing figure is Peter Schlesinger, his former partner, and the relationship had just ended, which the painting makes fairly obvious. It sold in 2018 for $90.3 million, then the record for a living artist, a record Hockney held until Jeff Koons took it months later.

title: Untitled Film Still #21
trivia: Sherman photographed herself as an imaginary career girl in a city, in a film that does not exist and never has, and the whole series works because viewers are certain they have seen the movie. She did her own hair, makeup, costumes and lighting, mostly alone with a shutter release. She made 69 of them between 1977 and 1980 and stopped when she felt the clichés had run out. MoMA bought the complete set in 1995.

title: Irony of a Negro Policeman
trivia: Basquiat was twenty and had been sleeping on friends' floors two years earlier, spraying cryptic SAMO slogans around downtown Manhattan with a school friend. Within another two years he was on the cover of the New York Times Magazine. The painting's target is the position of a Black man enforcing a system built against him, and the policeman's hat is drawn as a cage. He died of an overdose at 27.

title: Radiant Baby
trivia: Haring drew these in white chalk on the black paper that covered unsold advertising panels in the New York subway, sometimes forty a day, and was arrested repeatedly for it. Commuters recognised him and stopped to talk, which he said was the point: the audience came free. He later opened a shop selling his images cheaply on purpose, infuriating the art world, and died of AIDS-related illness in 1990 at 31.

title: Shulamite
trivia: Kiefer took the interior of a Nazi memorial hall designed for fallen soldiers and reworked it into a scorched, blackened crypt with a small flame at the far end, retitling it after a figure in Paul Celan's poem about the death camps. Kiefer's early work involved photographing himself performing the Nazi salute across Europe, which was received about as badly as you would expect and was intended to be.

title: Hollywood Africans
trivia: Painted after a trip to Los Angeles with two friends, the graffiti artists Toxic and Rammellzee, whose names appear on the canvas alongside a list of the roles Black actors were offered: sugar cane, tobacco, gangsterism. The words are crossed out, a device Basquiat used constantly and explained by saying that crossing something out makes you look at it more. The yellow ground is one of his brightest.

title: Rabbit
trivia: A cast of a cheap inflatable toy in mirror-polished stainless steel, so any photograph of it necessarily contains the photographer, and no reproduction of it can ever be neutral. It has no face. Koons had worked as a Wall Street commodities broker to fund his early production, and runs a large studio where he does not personally fabricate the objects. It sold in 2019 for $91.1 million, taking the living-artist record from Hockney.

title: Betty
trivia: Painted from a photograph Richter had taken of his daughter in 1978, ten years earlier, and she is turning away from the viewer and out of the picture. In the original photograph she was looking at one of his own grey abstract paintings. Richter has moved deliberately between photorealism and pure abstraction his whole career, refusing to settle, and has said he pursues no objectives, no system and no tendency.

title: Untitled (Your body is a battleground)
trivia: Made for a march on Washington in support of legal abortion, and produced as a poster before it was ever a gallery object. Kruger worked for a decade as a graphic designer at Condé Nast, and the Futura Bold Oblique in a red bar is straight out of magazine layout, which is exactly why it lands. The face is split into positive and negative halves of the same photograph.

title: Do Women Have To Be Naked To Get Into the Met. Museum?
trivia: Designed as a New York bus advertisement, and the bus company rejected it on the grounds that the image was too suggestive, which the Guerrilla Girls immediately pointed out was the entire argument. The group formed in 1985, wear gorilla masks in public, take the names of dead women artists as pseudonyms, and count works in museums. Their recount decades later found the numbers had barely improved.

title: The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living
trivia: Charles Saatchi paid £50,000, most of which went on catching and shipping a four-metre tiger shark from Australia. The formaldehyde was badly injected, the shark began to rot, and the skin was eventually stretched over a fibreglass mould, prompting a genuine philosophical argument about whether it was still the same artwork. It was replaced entirely with a new shark in 2006. Hirst said the point was that you cannot really imagine your own death.

title: House
trivia: Whiteread filled a condemned East London terraced house with concrete, then stripped away the brick shell, leaving a solid cast of the air people had lived inside. She won the Turner Prize for it and was simultaneously given a prize for worst artist by a rival group on the same evening. The local council voted to demolish it eleven weeks later, on the same day she won, and it was destroyed in January 1994.

title: Benefits Supervisor Sleeping
trivia: Freud worked in daily sittings over about nine months, and the sitter, Sue Tilley, was a performance artist and job centre supervisor introduced to him by a mutual friend. She has written cheerfully about the boredom and the fry-ups. Freud painted only from life, refused photographs, and was notorious for taking years over a single canvas. It sold in 2008 for $33.6 million, then a record for a living artist.

title: Angel of the North
trivia: Locals nicknamed it the Gateshead Flasher, a formal campaign opposed its construction, and a local newspaper ran a sustained hostile front-page effort against it. It is 20 metres tall with a wingspan wider than a jumbo jet, cast partly from Gormley's own body, and engineered to withstand winds of over 160 kph on a former colliery site. It now appears on regional tourist branding and roughly one in three people in England has seen it.

title: 99 Cent
trivia: Gursky digitally flattened the perspective so that the shelves recede without ever appearing to, an effect no single lens can produce, which is why the image feels subtly wrong before you work out why. He was a student of Bernd and Hilla Becher, whose deadpan industrial typologies trained a generation of German photographers. A version sold in 2007 for $3.3 million, briefly the most expensive photograph ever sold.

title: My Bed
trivia: Emin's actual bed, transported with the vodka bottles, cigarette packets, underwear and used condoms that surrounded it after several days of a breakdown. Shortlisted for the Turner Prize, where two Chinese performance artists stripped to the waist and jumped on it as their own uninvited work, and a woman turned up wanting to clean it. It sold in 2014 for £2.5 million. Emin has said she came back into the room, saw it, and recognised it as finished.

title: Girl with Balloon
trivia: First stencilled on a wall near Waterloo Bridge in London and painted over within a few years, like most of his early work. It was voted Britain's favourite artwork in a 2017 poll, beating Constable and Turner, which caused a certain amount of grinding of teeth. Banksy has reused the image for charity fundraising, including a version for Syrian refugees, and it functions now more as a logo than a painting.

title: The Weather Project
trivia: Two million people visited Tate Modern's Turbine Hall to lie on the floor and look at themselves in the mirrored ceiling, which was not what Eliasson had predicted they would do. The sun is a semicircle of monofrequency lamps completed by the mirror, and the mist was sugar and water. The lamps emit light at a single yellow wavelength, so everything in the hall appears in shades of yellow and black, and human faces look strange.

title: For the Love of God
trivia: A platinum cast of an eighteenth-century human skull set with 8,601 diamonds, with the original teeth put back into the jaw, and it cost around £14 million to make. The title comes from Hirst's mother, who reportedly asked what on earth he was going to do next. It was announced as sold for £50 million to an investment group that turned out to include Hirst himself, which prompted a certain amount of comment.

title: Sunflower Seeds
trivia: One hundred million porcelain seeds, each individually hand-painted by around 1,600 workers in Jingdezhen, a town that produced imperial porcelain for centuries and had been in economic decline. Visitors were initially allowed to walk on them until dust concerns closed the surface off. Sunflower seeds are a common Chinese snack and also propaganda imagery, with Mao as the sun and the people as seeds turning toward him.

title: You're Right and You Know It (And So Should Everyone Else)
trivia: A long, narrow strip nine inches high and twenty-four wide, published for the Editions and Artists Books Fair in New York in an edition of 200, each signed and numbered on the back. The image is a woman with an expression of open fear, and the text laid across it is completely certain of itself, which is the mechanism: Kruger spent over a decade as a designer and picture editor at Conde Nast, and she builds these the way a magazine builds a cover line, so the confidence reads as borrowed rather than earned. Her signature white Futura Bold Oblique on a red bar dates from 1981, and in 1994 Supreme's founder handed a designer a book of her work; the resulting box logo is the same typeface on the same red rectangle, and he later conceded in court filings that it came directly from her. She has never sued, telling the New Yorker in 2017 that she owns neither the typeface nor a logo. Then in 2013 Supreme sued a small womenswear label for $10 million over Supreme Bitch merchandise, and Complex asked Kruger for comment. She replied with a blank email and one attached Word document, named fools.doc, containing the line "What a ridiculous clusterfuck of totally uncool jokers" and a note that she was waiting for all of them to sue her for infringement. Bootleg hats and stickers bearing the acronym appeared within days. She later staged a pop-up shop titled Untitled (The Drop), parodying the weekly release model Supreme built its business on. This copy hangs in the owner's apartment.

title: The Artist Is Present
location: Museum of Modern Art, New York
trivia: AbramoviÄ‡ sat silently at a table in MoMA for 736 hours over three months, opposite whoever chose to sit down, and more than 1,500 people did, some queuing overnight. Many cried. On the opening day her former partner Ulay, with whom she had ended a twelve-year relationship in 1988 by walking toward each other from opposite ends of the Great Wall of China, sat down unannounced, and she broke the rules to take his hands.

title: This Is Fine
location: published online in the strip Gunshow
trivia: Two panels from a six-panel strip: a dog in a hat sits in a burning room with a coffee cup and says everything is fine. What the meme cuts off is the rest of the strip, in which the dog's face melts and it dies. Green has been openly uneasy about the crop, partly because the ending is the point and partly because the image gets used by exactly the institutions it satirises, including a US political party account during the 2016 election, which prompted him to say publicly that they should stop. He later drew a sequel in which the dog gets up and puts the fire out. Nobody shares that one.

title: Untitled (Studio)
location: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
trivia: Marshall paints his figures in an unmixed, near-absolute black, arguing that the Western canon simply has no vocabulary for Black skin and that he intends to supply one rather than negotiate with the existing palette. The painting shows a photographer's studio, a space where images of Black people are deliberately constructed. He has spent his career filling what he calls a vacuum in the museum, and the Met bought this one directly.

title: Love Is in the Bin
medium: spray paint and acrylic on canvas
trivia: The canvas shredded itself seconds after the hammer fell at Sotheby's on a £1.04 million sale, via a mechanism Banksy had built into the frame years earlier. It was supposed to shred completely and jammed halfway, which he later admitted in a video. The buyer went through with the purchase, the work was renamed, and it resold in 2021 for £18.6 million, roughly eighteen times the price it destroyed itself over.

title: Comedian
medium: banana, duct tape and certificate of authenticity
trivia: A banana taped to a wall at an art fair in Miami, in an edition of three, two of which sold at $120,000 each. What the buyer receives is a certificate and a set of instructions specifying the tape angle and the replacement interval, because the banana is a consumable. Within days a performance artist pulled it off the wall and ate it in front of the crowd, and the gallery simply taped up another one from a fruit stand down the road, which proved the point better than the work had. Cattelan had spent weeks trying to sculpt a banana in resin and bronze before concluding that an actual banana was funnier. A later edition sold at auction for several million to a cryptocurrency executive, who also ate it.

title: Untitled (Collage)
medium: magazine and mixed media on canvas

personal_copy.related_work_owned: one of three ceramic books containing excerpts from her collages

trivia: Caspe was born on Nantucket in 2001, took a BA at Roger Williams University and then a ceramics MA at the Royal College of Art, finishing in 2024, and this collage comes out of that London year rather than from the surreal coil-built figures she is better known for. She has said that growing up on an island is what made her curious about everywhere else, and the travel since has fed the textures and the stories in the sculptures. She also runs a non-profit, The Bowl That Keeps on Giving, which sells art to fund food for malnourished children, and presented it at an international arts conference in Poland in 2023, which is a more useful thing to have done at 22 than most graduate shows manage. She later made three small ceramic books holding excerpts from her collages; one of them is in the owner's collection.
